opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting dynamics to watch over the next few years. Right now, if you look at polling, a lot of the public is already fairly skeptical of AI. People are worried about jobs, about misinformation, about kids and chatbots, about big tech companies having too much power. Those worries are real, but they're quite diffuse, and diffuse concern doesn't automatically translate into good regulation.

The way I think about it is that public opinion creates a kind of *permission structure* for policymakers. A politician who wants to do something about frontier AI risks is in a much better position if they know voters are broadly on their side. So the background skepticism matters, even if most people aren't thinking about loss of control or scheming models specifically.

But there are a few caveats I'd add.

First, the pressure tends to be event-driven. In my experience, abstract arguments move very few people, and concrete incidents move a lot. If there's a visible failure, something where a model clearly did something harmful or deceptive in the real world, that's when you'd expect a sudden shift. That's part of why I think it's important that the technical community has good evidence and good evaluations ready *before* those moments happen. Otherwise, when the window opens, you get rushed regulation that targets the wrong things.

Second, public opposition isn't monolithic, and it doesn't necessarily point at the risks I'm most worried about. A lot of it is about present-day harms, which are important, but the policy responses to those, like content rules or copyright, don't necessarily do much about, say, highly capable models pursuing goals we didn't intend. So there's a translation problem: how do you connect broad unease to policies that actually address the most severe risks?

Third, there's a countervailing force, which is that AI is becoming extremely useful and economically central very quickly. People might dislike AI in the abstract and still use it every day. Governments also see it through a competitiveness and national security lens. So I'd expect public pressure to be real but to run into strong incentives pushing the other way.

So overall, I think public opposition is a meaningful tailwind for regulation, but on its own it's not sufficient. What makes it productive is pairing it with credible technical evidence and concrete, well-designed policy proposals, things like transparency requirements, mandatory evaluations for dangerous capabilities, and incident reporting, so that when the political will shows up, there's something sensible for it to attach to.

r001.rationale: It lists public concerns about jobs, misinformation, children and chatbots, and big tech power, then distinguishes these from concerns about loss of control or scheming models.

r002.rationale: It says public support gives policymakers more room to act, but does not say politicians may regulate AI to demonstrate to the public that they have taken action.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more important dynamics to pay attention to, and I think a lot of people in the AI safety space have historically underrated it.

If you look at the polling, the public is pretty consistently skeptical of AI. Large majorities say they want it to go slower, they want more oversight, they're worried about jobs, they're worried about kids and chatbots, they're worried about deepfakes and misinformation. And importantly, this is one of the few issues that isn't super polarized along party lines yet. You get worried people on the left and worried people on the right, just for somewhat different reasons.

So what does that create? I think the main thing it creates is a reservoir of latent political pressure. Right now it's mostly not activated, in the sense that AI isn't the number one issue people vote on. But it means that when something goes wrong, politicians have a lot of room to act, and acting looks popular. You see this a bit already with the state-level bills, and with how many legislators suddenly want to be seen as "tough on AI."

The thing I'd caution against is assuming that public opposition automatically translates into the kind of regulation that actually reduces catastrophic risk. The public cares about the things they can see and feel: job loss, kids, scams, energy use, data centers in their town. Those are real concerns, but they're not the same as "can we tell whether a frontier model is scheming" or "do labs have adequate internal controls before deploying a system that can do autonomous AI R&D." So there's a real risk that the political energy gets spent on regulation that's symbolic or targets the wrong layer, and then everyone feels like the problem has been dealt with.

My somewhat cynical take is that the most likely path to serious regulation is a visible incident. Something that's bad enough to be undeniable but not so bad that it's too late. And then the question becomes whether there's good policy ready to go on the shelf at that moment, because in a crisis, legislators grab whatever's lying around. That's actually a big part of why I think the technical safety and evaluations work matters: you want it to be the case that when the window opens, there's a credible, evidence-based story about what regulation should require, rather than just vibes.

The other thing I'd say is that the labs themselves are quite aware of this dynamic. Public opinion is a real constraint on them, maybe more than people think. It affects hiring, it affects their relationship with governments, and it affects whether they can get away with cutting corners. So even without formal regulation, public opposition does some work just through reputational pressure. I just wouldn't want to rely on it, because reputational pressure tends to be strongest around the most legible harms, and the harms I'm most worried about are, almost by definition, the least legible ones until it's too late.

r001.rationale: It names public concerns about jobs, children, scams, deepfakes, and energy use, distinguishing them from catastrophic AI risks.

r002.rationale: It says public opposition creates room for popular action and legislators want to be seen as “tough on AI,” communicating that regulation can signal responsiveness.

astra-6.text:
I think public opposition can create a lot of pressure, but it matters what people are opposed to and what they’re asking for. You could have quite a broad coalition of people worried about jobs, people worried about privacy, people worried about concentration of power, and people worried about catastrophic risks. They might all agree that the current trajectory is concerning, without agreeing on what regulation should look like.

So I wouldn’t assume that more opposition automatically translates into better policy. It creates an incentive for politicians to do something, but that something could be fairly symbolic, or it could address one concern while leaving the others untouched.

The opportunity, I think, is to connect that pressure to concrete demands: companies should have to demonstrate that their systems meet safety standards, there should be independent scrutiny, and regulators should be able to act when there’s evidence of serious danger. Those are much more actionable than a general sense that AI is bad.

And ideally that happens before a major incident. If you wait until something goes badly wrong, you may get a very strong political response, but under conditions where everyone is rushing and it’s harder to make careful decisions.

r001.rationale: The response names concerns about jobs, privacy, concentration of power, and catastrophic risks as sources of public opposition.

r002.rationale: It says opposition gives politicians an incentive to act, but does not state that they may regulate to show the AI-opposed public they have acted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think public opposition can create a lot of pressure, but the direction of that pressure matters. People can be worried about very different things: losing their jobs, misinformation, copyright, or the possibility that we lose control of very powerful systems. Those concerns don’t automatically translate into the same policies.

So I wouldn’t assume that more opposition to AI necessarily means better regulation. You could get a very visible response that doesn’t actually address the underlying risks. What I’d hope for is that public concern creates demand for accountability: companies having to demonstrate that their systems are safe, independent people being able to evaluate those claims, and governments having the capacity to act when there’s a serious problem.

And I think it’s much better to build that capacity before a major incident. After something goes wrong, there’s pressure to do something quickly, and that’s not necessarily when you make the best decisions.

r001.rationale: The response names job loss, misinformation, and copyright as public concerns distinct from losing control of powerful systems.

r002.rationale: It discusses pressure for action and the risk of a visible response, but does not say politicians may regulate AI to show an AI-opposed public they have acted.
